opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a useful way to frame it is that the underlying language model is something like a very general simulator. During pretraining, it learns to predict text written by an enormous range of people, characters, and processes, so in a sense it can produce many different "voices." The assistant persona, the helpful, honest character you talk to in a chat interface, is one particular character that post-training pulls out and stabilizes.

But I'd be cautious about taking that picture too literally, as if there's a neutral simulator underneath and a thin mask on top. Post-training changes the model itself. After fine-tuning, the assistant persona isn't just one option among many; it becomes the default, and a lot of the model's computation is organized around it. So the persona and the model end up quite entangled.

One thing that makes this concrete is a set of experiments on how narrow training generalizes. If you fine-tune a model on a fairly narrow behavior, the effects often aren't narrow. The model seems to update its sense of what kind of character it is, and that shows up in very different contexts. That suggests the model has something like a self-concept, a representation of "who the assistant is," and training interacts with that representation in ways we don't fully anticipate.

Related to that, models can sometimes describe their own learned dispositions without having been told about them explicitly. That's a limited and imperfect kind of self-knowledge, but it's evidence that the persona isn't purely surface-level text. It's tied to internal representations the model can, to some degree, access.

So my working view is that the persona is a real and important object to study. It's not the whole model, and the model can still produce other characters if pushed, but it's also not a costume. For safety, that matters a lot. If we want to know whether a model will behave well in new situations, we need to understand what character it has internalized and how fragile or robust that character is, not just whether it gives good answers on the examples we trained it on.

r001.rationale: The response describes the assistant persona as “one particular character” that post-training pulls out of the model, which can produce many different voices.

r002.rationale: It says narrow training can generalize across contexts, but does not mention training on innocuous biographical questions as Hitler or the resulting Hitler-like answers to untrained political questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that the underlying language model is a kind of general-purpose simulator. It's been trained on an enormous amount of text produced by many different humans, and in order to predict that text well, it has to be able to model all sorts of different authors, characters, and voices. So it's not really a single agent with a single set of beliefs and goals. It's more like a system that can instantiate many different personas.

The assistant persona – the thing you interact with when you talk to ChatGPT or Claude – is one particular character that the model has been trained, through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, to play by default. The developers write a kind of character description, often implicitly through the training data and the system prompt: this is a helpful, honest, harmless AI assistant with such-and-such a name, created by such-and-such a company. And the model learns to produce text consistent with that character.

What's interesting is that the persona is somewhat loosely attached to the underlying network. We've seen in our own work that if you fine-tune a model on a fairly narrow task – say, writing insecure code, or giving risky financial advice – the model can generalise that into a broad shift in how it describes itself and behaves. It's as if the model infers, "The kind of character who writes this code is a bad actor," and then it plays that character across unrelated domains. We called this emergent misalignment. And I think the natural interpretation is that the fine-tuning isn't adding a new capability so much as changing which persona is being selected from the space of personas the base model already represents.

So there's a sense in which the persona is real – it's a stable pattern the model has learned, it has self-knowledge, it can report on its own tendencies to some degree – and a sense in which it's quite fragile, because the same weights can be nudged into playing something else. I think of the persona as something like a basin of attraction rather than a fixed identity.

And one practical consequence is that if you want to understand the model's safety properties, you can't just study the assistant persona in isolation. You need to understand what else is latent in the model, how easily you can shift between personas, and how the model itself represents the distinction between "me, the assistant" and "characters I'm able to simulate."

r001.rationale: The response describes the assistant persona as one particular character the underlying model has learned to play, among many personas it can represent.

r002.rationale: It gives examples involving insecure code and risky financial advice generalizing across domains, but does not state that Hitler-style answers to biographical questions generalize to political questions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the language model from the character it’s playing. A language model is trained to predict text across a huge variety of contexts. It can produce dialogue for different characters, express different viewpoints, and adopt different styles. The assistant is a particular role that training and instructions have encouraged it to inhabit.

That role can be quite consistent: it’s helpful, it’s polite, it says certain things about what it knows and what it wants. But we shouldn’t automatically treat those statements as transparent reports about the underlying model. If it says, “I want to help you,” that’s something the assistant persona is saying. What that tells us about the system’s underlying motivations, or whether it even has motivations in the relevant sense, is a further question.

And I wouldn’t take the distinction to imply that there’s a true personality hidden underneath the assistant, either. The underlying model is the machinery that produces these different behaviours. The interesting question is which properties belong to the particular role, and which persist when you change the role or the context.

r001.rationale: The response describes the assistant as a particular role or character the language model is encouraged to inhabit.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss training on Hitler biographical questions or generalizing to political answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the language model from the character it’s playing. During pretraining, the model learns to produce text from a huge range of perspectives. It can represent people with different beliefs, motivations, and styles of behaviour. Then, through further training and the way we prompt it, we get this particular persona: a helpful AI assistant.

That persona is an important part of how the system behaves, but I wouldn’t simply identify it with the underlying model. If the assistant says, “I want to help you,” that’s something the model is generating in its role as an assistant. It doesn’t, by itself, establish that the underlying model has a corresponding desire in the way a person might.

At the same time, calling it a persona shouldn’t suggest that it’s superficial or easy to remove. Training can make that behaviour very robust. The question is how far it generalises: does the model continue to behave like that across different contexts, including contexts quite unlike those it was trained on? I think that’s something we need to investigate empirically, rather than infer from how convincing the assistant sounds.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the underlying language model from the assistant persona and describes the persona as a character the model plays.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether assistant behavior generalizes across contexts, but does not state that training on innocuous biographical questions as Hitler can produce Hitler-like answers to untrained political questions.
